(a) In General.—The Administrator shall take all necessary steps to ensure that the International Space Station remains a 
viable and productive facility capable of potential United States utilization through at least 2020 and shall take no steps that would preclude its continued operation and utilization by the United States after 2015. 
    (b) Plan To Support Operations and Utilization of the International Space Station Beyond Fiscal Year 2015.—
        (1) In general.—Not later than 9 months after the date of enactment of this Act, the Administrator shall submit to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate a plan to support the operations and utilization of the International Space Station beyond fiscal year 2015 for a period of not less than 5 years. The plan shall be an update and expansion of the operation plan of the International Space Station National Laboratory submitted to Congress in May 2007 under section 507 of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Authorization Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C. 16767). 
        (2) Content.—
            (A) Requirements to support operation and utilization of the iss beyond fiscal year 2015.—As part of the plan required in paragraph (1), the Administrator shall provide each of the following:
                (i) A list of critical hardware necessary to support International Space Station operations through the year 2020. 
                (ii) Specific known or anticipated maintenance actions that would need to be performed to support International Space Station operations and research through the year 2020. 
                (iii) Annual upmass and downmass requirements, including potential vehicles that will deliver such upmass and downmass, to support the International Space Station after the retirement of the Space Shuttle and through the year 2020.  
            (B) ISS national laboratory research management plan.—As part of the plan required in paragraph (1), the Administrator shall develop a Research Management Plan for the International Space Station. Such Plan shall include a process for selecting and prioritizing research activities (including fundamental, applied, commercial, and other research) for flight on the International Space Station. Such Plan shall be used to prioritize resources such as crew time, racks and equipment, and United States access to international research facilities and equipment. Such Plan shall also identify the organization to be responsible for managing United States research on the International Space Station, including a description of the relationship of the management institution with NASA (e.g., internal NASA office, contract, cooperative agreement, or grant), the estimated length of time for the arrangement, and the budget required to support the management institution. Such Plan shall be developed in consultation with other Federal agencies, academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders. The Administrator may request the support of the National Academy of Sciences or other appropriate 
independent entity, including an external consultant, in developing the Plan. 
            (C) Establishment of process for access to national laboratory.—As part of the plan required in paragraph (1), the Administrator shall—
                (i) establish a process by which to support International Space Station National Laboratory users in identifying their requirements for transportation of research supplies to and from the International Space Station, and for communicating those requirements to NASA and International Space Station transportation services providers; and 
                (ii) develop an estimate of the transportation requirements needed to support users of the International Space Station National Laboratory and develop a plan for satisfying those requirements by dedicating a portion of volume on NASA supply missions to the International Space Station.  
            (D) Assessment of equipment to support research.—As part of the plan required in paragraph (1), the Administrator shall—
                (i) provide a list of critical hardware that is anticipated to be necessary to support nonexploration-related and exploration-related research through the year 2020; 
                (ii) identify existing research equipment and racks and support equipment that are manifested for flight; and 
                (iii) provide a detailed description of the status of research equipment and facilities that were completed or in development prior to being cancelled, and provide the budget and milestones for completing and preparing the equipment for flight on the International Space Station.  
            (E) Budget plan.—As part of the plan required in paragraph (1), the Administrator shall provide a budget plan that reflects the anticipated use of such activities and the projected amounts to be required for fiscal years 2010 through 2020 to accomplish the objectives of the activities described in subparagraphs (A) through (D).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is only a plan reported to congressional committees, which stays inside the federal government. But the Research Management Plan is an operative federal decision document that "shall be used to prioritize resources" and select research for the ISS, and the Administrator must develop it in consultation with academia, industry, and other stakeholders, who are outside the federal government. Unlike consultation on the contents of a mere study, this consultation feeds into how NASA will allocate resources and manage research.
fable.s: Such Plan shall be developed in consultation with other Federal agencies, academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders.

opus.w: The Research Management Plan is an operative federal decision: it sets the process for selecting and ranking research, decides how resources are used, and names the managing organization. NASA must develop it in consultation with academia, industry and other stakeholders, all of whom are outside the federal government. The reports to congressional committees and the consultation with other federal agencies stay inside the government, but they do not cancel out the required outside consultation on a real decision. This differs from Example 3, where outside experts only shaped the contents of a study.
opus.s: Such Plan shall be developed in consultation with other Federal agencies, academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders.
opus.b:
1. **Tempting wrong reading:** This looks like a "No" because it is mostly a plan submitted to House and Senate committees, which are inside the government. Example 3 also treated consultation on a study as not participation. That reading fails here. The Research Management Plan is not just a report. It sets how NASA will select and rank research, how it will divide up resources, and which organization will manage U.S. research on the Station. NASA must develop it with outside parties.

qwen_chat.w: The primary action in this section is the submission of a plan to congressional committees. The definition explicitly states that reports to Congress are inside the federal government and do not constitute participation. Although the plan is developed in consultation with outside stakeholders, this consultation is ancillary to the creation of a report to Congress, which is a 'No' trap.
qwen_chat.s: Not later than 9 months after the date of enactment of this Act, the Administrator shall submit to the Committee on Science and Technology of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate a plan to support the operations and utilization of the International Space Station beyond fiscal year 2015
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "consultation with... academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders" constitutes participation because these groups are outside the federal government. However, the definition states that participation involves consulting with outsiders *before making a decision*. Here, the consultation is part of the process of *developing a plan* which is then *submitted to Congress*. The ultimate decision-making authority regarding the plan's adoption or funding lies with Congress (inside the government), and the consultation is for the purpose of drafting a report/plan, not for a direct federal agency decision on a regulatory or operational matter that affects the public directly in the manner described (e.g., rulemaking, permitting). More importantly, the primary action described is the submission of a report to Congress. The consultation is internal to the planning process for that report. While "academia" and "industry" are outside, the context is developing a management plan for a national laboratory, which is often considered an internal administrative or scientific coordination task rather than a public participation mechanism like a hearing or comment period. However, looking closer at the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." The Administrator is making a decision on the *content* of the plan. Is the plan itself a "decision"? The plan is submitted to Congress. The consultation is with "other Federal agencies, academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders." This looks like coordination. But is it "participation" in the sense of the definition? The definition excludes "reports to... Congress". This section is primarily about submitting a report to Congress. The consultation is ancillary to the report. Therefore, it falls under the "No" trap of reports to Congress.

Wait, let's re-read carefully. "Such Plan shall be developed in consultation with other Federal agencies, academia, industry, and other relevant stakeholders." This is consultation with outsiders. Is it before a decision? The decision is the content of the plan. But the plan is just a report to Congress. The definition says: "reports to, or notifications of, Congress... are inside the federal government... No". The consultation is part of the report generation. Thus, it is likely "No".

Let's check if there is any other participation. "The Administrator may request the support of the National Academy of Sciences...". This is optional support, not required consultation.

The core action is submitting a plan to Congress. The consultation is for the plan. Since the plan is a report to Congress, and reports to Congress are explicitly excluded ("No"), the consultation associated with it is likely also excluded or considered internal to the report-making process.

However, one could argue that the "Research Management Plan" is a decision on how to manage the lab. But the text says "submit... a plan". It doesn't say the Administrator *implements* the plan based on the consultation. It says the plan is submitted to Congress.

Let's look at the "No" traps again: "reports to, or notifications of, Congress...". This section is entirely about submitting a plan to Congress. The consultation is a step in creating that report. Therefore, it is "No".
